nodes.statement: Avoid very shallow taper ratios such as 1:64 for S-lay overbend passage unless checked by dedicated analysis.
Check thick-body BM independently from pipeline strain in C1 layouts.
Check adjacent-pipe strain and component-body BM separately for long thick sections.
Treat wall-thickness increase as a strain-increasing design change, even when needed for strength.
For long structural zones, evaluate single-roller versus dual-roller contact before applying a monotonic length rule.
Treat peak pipeline strain and peak component bending moment as separate checks because they govern at different locations.
Treat very long shroud strain relief as a contact-regime effect that needs verification, not a general rule that longer shrouds are safer.
Use GD-SH taper length L2 for geometry/fabrication/passage needs; Paper 1 shows little direct strain sensitivity.
Do not over-optimize normal-range GD-SH deep-section length L1 for strain reduction without additional evidence.
Treat code-minimum geometry as a compliance boundary rather than automatically strain-optimal conceptual geometry.
Do not rely on spacing as the main strain-reduction mechanism for short repeated GD-TP components in the tested range.
For GD-SH concept screening, focus response checks on X2 while retaining X3/X4 as spatial evidence rows.
Keep GD-TP out of the shroud X2 catenary-side region where possible.
Avoid long thick-pipe lengths inside GD-SH unless dedicated C1 analysis confirms acceptability.
Minimize GD-SH offset depth V where possible; V is the dominant isolated shroud strain driver.
Minimize unnecessary GD-TP length in overbend-critical regions.
Keep pipeline strain checks and component-body bending-moment checks as separate acceptance paths.
Store source location and response location separately in EDIKB; where a feature is placed can govern response as much as what the feature is.
For conceptual overbend screening of a GD-TT-like tapered transition, use 1:4 as the default taper unless fabrication, fit-up, or project constraints justify longer taper.
Use EDAS/EDIKB assembly behaviour rules for combined mechanisms instead of adding isolated EDES responses.
Use dedicated C1 rules for nested shroud + thick-pipe assemblies.
Use Paper 1 evidence for concept ranking, feature selection, and ML seed rules; require refined analysis for final code compliance.
Treat P_gap as a tuning parameter that moves strain, not as a generic strain-reduction device.
For EA-SB, rank designs by both internal low-strain pocket value and maximum shifted/high-strain value.
Do not apply EA-ST's F1/PS low-disturbance guidance to EA-SB. For base structures, PS remains a high-local-strain option.
Choose F1 or PS when the top structure should behave close to plain pipe and should not significantly disturb the surrounding header strain field.

Choose F2, F2D or PSD when a low-strain internal region is needed for strain-sensitive equipment, while managing strain at or near connector regions. Differentiate the systems by pocket magnitude and high-strain penalty: F2 creates a very low pocket but the highest connector penalty; F2D and PSD keep/produce low pockets while redistributing the penalty.

nodes.label: Check interaction evidence before summing component effects
nodes.statement: For full layouts, retrieve combined assembly rules and interaction candidates before estimating total response from individual components.
nodes.designUse: The solver should decompose the layout, retrieve isolated effects, search for combined evidence, and only then decide whether a cautious additive estimate or future FEA/ML candidate is appropriate.
nodes.caution: Do not present component-effect summation as proven when direct combined evidence is missing.

nodes.statement: For long GD-TP components, peak BM can keep increasing while peak pipeline strain flattens.
Component length is the dominant GD-TP parameter for peak pipeline strain.
For GD-TP thick-section-only cases, peak strain occurs at pipe-to-component junction and peak BM near midspan.
For two identical short GD-TP components, increasing spacing gives only negligible strain reduction.
For short thick-pipe components, increasing wall thickness ratio increases peak pipeline strain moderately and near-linearly.
Peak bending moment for tapered transitions occurs in the thick body while peak strain occurs outside the taper zone.
For tapered transition cases, peak pipeline strain occurs at the straight-pipe/transition junction.
Within the DNV-compliant taper range 1:4 to 1:16, peak pipeline strain changes by less than 5%.
A very shallow 1:64 taper causes a step-change increase in peak strain.
Very long GD-SH lengths can trigger dual-roller contact and reduce X2 peak strain relative to shorter single-roller support cases.
nodes.limitations: Sparse evidence; long-shroud benefit depends on support/contact regime and should not be generalized without additional studies.

nodes.statement: For normal GD-SH deep-section lengths from 2.5D to 10D, L1 has little influence on X2 peak pipeline strain compared with offset depth V.
nodes.limitations: Only a few L1 cases; results may change with pipe OD, WT, roller spacing, or shroud-contact geometry.

nodes.statement: GD-SH taper length L2 has negligible effect on X2 peak pipeline strain in the tested cases.
nodes.limitations: Only two direct L2 cases at one L1/V/R/T combination.

nodes.statement: GD-SH Type B1 peak pipeline strain occurs in Phase 2 for all reported isolated shroud cases.
nodes.limitations: Only Paper 1 Type B1 isolated shroud cases.

nodes.statement: GD-SH Type B1 response is spatially graded: X2 is governing, X3 is intermediate, and X4 is lowest with a plateau-like response at larger V.
nodes.limitations: Region distributions reported for one R/T/L1/L2 setup only.

nodes.statement: For isolated GD-SH Type B1, offset depth V is the dominant parameter and increases X2 peak pipeline strain approximately monotonically over the tested range.
nodes.limitations: Single pipeline geometry; roller spacing fixed at 9 m; V trend is not a full-factorial study across all L1/L2 values.

nodes.statement: Plain-pipe peak strain is governed by Phase 1 in all baseline cases tested.
Increasing stinger radius reduces plain-pipe peak overbend strain monotonically.
Applied top tension increases peak strain relative to no-tension cases for tested pipe diameters.
GD-TP location inside GD-SH is critical; X2 placement is worse than X3/X4.
Combined GD-SH + GD-TP response exceeds isolated component types and should not be estimated by simple addition.
C1 peak pipeline strain remains at X2 regardless of thick-pipe location; X2 source placement produces pipe/component-junction peak at X2.
C1 combined cases govern in Phase 2, inherited from the shroud/elevation mechanism.
Increasing thick-pipe length inside the shroud substantially increases C1 peak strain and BM.
Long structural zones can relieve peak strain when they span enough roller spacing to force dual-roller contact.
nodes.limitations: Roller spacing is fixed in Paper 1, so independent spacing effect remains untested.

nodes.statement: Assembly-level strain for combined mechanisms should not be estimated by simple addition of isolated EDES component responses.
nodes.limitations: Only GD-SH + GD-TP C1 assembly tested.

nodes.statement: Across Paper 1 mechanical types, source position relative to the catenary-side response region governs peak strain as much as feature magnitude.
nodes.limitations: Synthesized from A1/B1/C1 only; A2/B2/C2 not yet covered.

nodes.statement: Paper 1 numeric evidence should be used as relative parametric design intuition, not as direct final code-compliance values.
nodes.limitations: Not a mechanical rule; it is a data-use constraint.

nodes.statement: Pipeline strain and component-body bending moment can diverge; a layout favourable for pipeline strain may still raise component bending demand.
nodes.limitations: Most direct evidence comes from GD-TP length studies.

nodes.label: Added mass installation behaviour
nodes.summary: Assembly-level added mass increases installation strain; for the tested 40 MT cases, mass location matters more than short-range point distribution.

nodes.label: EA-ST system governs header strain ranking
nodes.statement: F2 gives the lowest branch strain but the highest header strain, while PS keeps header strain near baseline with moderate branch strain.
nodes.evidence_status: direct numeric branch cases in Paper 2

nodes.label: Header and branch strain are partly separable
nodes.statement: Branch pipe strain is mainly controlled by branch support connector type, while header pipeline strain is mainly controlled by the EA-ST connection system and connector spacing.
nodes.evidence_status: supported by L and Z branch numeric cases; needs wider geometry sweep

nodes.label: Branch piping layout behaviour
nodes.summary: Branch topology, branch support connector type, and EA-ST connection system jointly determine header and branch strain responses.

nodes.label: Missing Z-branch slotted cases
nodes.reason: Paper 2 covers L fixed/slotted comparisons but only fixed-to-top Z branch cases.

nodes.label: Slotted branch support lowers branch strain
nodes.statement: Replacing a fixed branch support with a slotted branch support lowers branch pipe strain, and may also reduce header strain depending on the EA-ST connection system.
nodes.evidence_status: six L-branch fixed/slot numeric comparisons; Z slotted cases missing

nodes.label: Connector offset and boss/bulkhead effects
nodes.reason: Paper 2 modelled connectors at pipe centreline; real connectors typically attach through bosses or bulkhead-like details.

nodes.label: EA-SB connector system controls strain through contact-owning base load path
nodes.statement: EA-SB pipeline strain is governed by connection system, base geometry and stiffness, with roller contact transferred through the base frame and connector load path.

nodes.label: EA-SB deadband redistributes strain
nodes.statement: For EA-SB, deadband systems reduce connector-region strain relative to plain F1/F2 systems but redistribute strain into internal or external regions.

nodes.label: EA-SB F2 stiffness plus elevation comparison with GD-TP plus GD-SH
nodes.statement: Study correlation of EA-SB F2 combined stiffness and base elevation/contact geometry with pipeline strain, and compare against GD-TP stiffness-ratio effects plus GD-SH elevation/depth effects.
nodes.reason: EA-SB F2 combines a stiff base-frame path with local elevation/contact transfer; current Paper 1 and Paper 2 evidence are related but not directly equivalent.

nodes.label: EA-SB connection systems create high strain penalties
nodes.statement: EA-SB connection systems should be compared by maximum reported regional strain and increment over plain-pipe baseline; all extracted EA-SB cases exceed the plain-pipe upper baseline in at least one region.

nodes.label: EA-SB can create low internal strain pockets with high shifted penalties
nodes.statement: EA-SB F2, F2D, PS and PSD systems can create low internal strain pockets, but usually with high connector-region or shifted strain elsewhere.

pocketClassification.tradeoff: severe X_c strain, 2.24 percent to 2.53 percent
X_c reduced relative to F2, strain shifted to X_i2 and X_e
X_i2 and X_e remain elevated around 0.83-0.84 percent

nodes.label: EA-SB PS is not plain-like
nodes.statement: Unlike EA-ST, EA-SB with PS connection does not keep the pipeline close to the plain-pipe strain field; it behaves closer to F2 with high local strain and a low internal pocket.

nodes.label: EA-SB PS comparison with GD-SH similar depth
nodes.statement: Compare EA-SB PS response with GD-SH cases of similar depth/elevation, especially P_v=2D versus shroud_V=2D, while preserving the different load paths.
nodes.reason: EA-SB PS has base contact ownership plus connector-mediated load transfer, whereas GD-SH is contact-only. Similar depth may not imply similar strain behaviour.

nodes.label: EA-SB local elevation may interact with GD-SH-style curvature control
nodes.statement: EA-SB locally elevates/redirects the pipeline contact path through base geometry and connector-mediated load transfer. This may interact with GD-SH-like elevation/curvature-control effects, and multi-roller support may reduce local strain concentration.
nodes.designUse: May be proposed by EDPR as a future analysis action when EA-SB local strain is excessive; should not be used as proven mitigation without supporting evidence rows.

nodes.label: EA-ST connector system controls header strain pattern
nodes.statement: EA-ST changes pipeline response through discrete connector load paths; response depends on active slots and connector types.

nodes.label: Deadband relocates EA-ST strain rather than removing it
nodes.statement: For EA-ST, adding deadband connectors redistributes strain away from the connector region into other internal or external regions, and the gap controls the relocation.

deadbandEncoding.note: Later solver output may add open/closed transition event rows.

nodes.label: Compare EA-ST F2 combined stiffness with GD-TT stiff-length behaviour
nodes.statement: Compare EA-ST F2 total frame+pipe stiffness over connector-to-connector distance with GD-TT stiffened length/stiffness increment at similar effective length.
nodes.reason: Current GD-TT rows contain stiffened/tapered lengths and responses, but no directly equivalent total frame+pipe stiffness ratio; record as future ML/FEA correlation study.

nodes.label: EA-ST connection systems create different high-strain penalties
nodes.statement: Connection systems should be compared by their maximum reported regional strain and the percentage increment over the plain-pipe baseline range.

nodes.label: Two-point EA-ST restraint creates low-strain internal pocket
nodes.statement: For EA-ST, two-point restraint systems can create a very low-strain zone inside the structure while increasing or redistributing strain near and outside connector regions.

pocketClassification.tradeoff: severe X_c and X_e strain penalty
strain shifted to X_i2 and X_e
moderate shifted strain in X_i2 and X_e

nodes.label: EA-ST has no direct roller-contact or section ownership
nodes.statement: EA-ST does not directly participate in roller contact or pipe-section ownership; installation-passage effects occur through connectors and attached structures.

nodes.label: F1 and PS keep EA-ST close to plain pipe
nodes.statement: For EA-ST, F1 and PS connection systems keep header-pipe strain close to the plain-pipe baseline.

nodes.label: Added mass location and distribution sweep
Added mass position dominates short distribution
nodes.statement: For the tested 40 MT added-mass case, location relative to the stinger rollers/span governs peak strain more strongly than whether the same mass is represented as one, two, or three nearby point masses.
nodes.evidence_status: three direct numeric cases; sparse for general regression

nodes.label: Superimpose Paper 1 thick-component effects
nodes.statement: External-attachment and branch-layout behaviour from Paper 2 should be combined with Paper 1 thick-component behaviour at connector/attachment points before absolute design checks.

nodes.label: Direct combined evidence overrides component superposition
nodes.statement: When a layout contains multiple interacting components, direct combined-case evidence must be preferred over summing or subtracting isolated component effects.
nodes.trend: combined response may be non-additive; direct combined evidence is higher priority than isolated component superposition

nodes.label: Simple superposition requires evidence or explicit assumption
nodes.statement: Adding or subtracting isolated component effects is only allowed when the solver records the operation as an evidence-backed relation or an explicit low-confidence conceptual assumption.
nodes.trend: absence of combined evidence should create an InteractionEffectCandidate or MLStudyCandidate rather than a confident additive estimate
